1.title: An alphabet of grief
1.text: Chapters 1, 2, and 4 of Lamentations are acrostics: each has 22 verses, one for every letter of the Hebrew alphabet — a poetic way of saying the grief is complete, from A to Z.

1.question: Why has the Lord afflicted the city (Lamentations 1:5)?
options: For the multitude of her transgressions
Because of the broken covenant with Egypt
Because of the hardness of her priests' hearts
Out of envy of neighboring nations

1.question: In Lamentations 1:12 the city calls to those who pass by to behold what?
options: The destruction of her sacred holy temple
If there is any sorrow like her sorrow
The greatness of the invading enemy armies
The end of her long captivity

1.question: What does the city confess about the Lord in Lamentations 1:18?
options: The Lord will soon deliver her from the yoke of her oppressors
The Lord has forgotten forever all of her past transgressions and sins
The Lord is righteous, for she rebelled against his commandment
The Lord will reward her with great and lasting glory

2.question: How does Lamentations 2:5 describe the Lord's dealings with Israel?
options: He became as an enemy
He became as a redeemer
He became as a faithful protector
As a faithful guardian

2.question: According to Lamentations 2:9, what is said of her prophets?
options: They receive false visions from idols
They find no vision from the Lord
They proclaim great victories that never come
They fled to the land of Egypt

2.question: In Lamentations 2:15, passersby mockingly recall that Jerusalem was called what?
options: The impregnable city that would never be conquered
The eternal fortress that the Lord would always defend
The perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth
The sacred gate that always led to heaven

2.question: What does Lamentations 2:17 say the Lord has done?
options: Restored at once the lost glory of his holy temple
Forgiven completely all the transgressions of his people
Hidden his face forever from his congregation
Fulfilled his word that he commanded in days of old

2.title: When prophecy goes silent
2.text: Verse 9 mourns that 'the law is no more' and the prophets 'find no vision' — for an Israelite, losing the temple meant losing the very channels through which God had spoken.

3.question: How does the speaker describe himself in Lamentations 3:1?
options: The man that has seen affliction by the rod of God's wrath
A priest who lost all of his sacred inheritance and honor
A watchman who proclaimed the holy city's imminent downfall
A prince of Judah carried captive to Babylon

3.question: In Lamentations 3:6, God set him in dark places, like whom?
options: Rulers of ancient empires
Those long dead
Prophets who foretold doom
Watching angels above

3.question: To what two animals does Lamentations 3:10 compare the Lord's dealings?
options: A swift eagle and a venomous serpent
A hungry wolf and a swift leopard
A bear lying in wait and a lion
A wild ox and a raging goat

3.question: What did God fill the speaker with, in Lamentations 3:15?
options: Pure honey and sweet wine
Fresh bread and clean water
Sacred oil and myrrh
Bitterness and wormwood

3.title: Great is thy faithfulness
3.text: Lamentations 3:22-23 — 'his compassions fail not. They are new every morning' — became the refrain of the beloved hymn 'Great Is Thy Faithfulness.' The book's deepest hope sits at its very center.

3.question: Lamentations 3:27 says it is good for a man to bear what in his youth?
options: The yoke
The sword
The crown
The staff

3.question: According to Lamentations 3:33, the Lord does not afflict the children of men how?
options: Forever
Willingly
In secret
Without warning

3.question: Lamentations 3:37 asks: who can speak and have it come to pass unless whom commands it?
options: The king
The prophet
The Lord
The priest

3.question: Lamentations 3:39 asks why a living man should complain, given what?
options: The brevity of earthly life
The prolonged silence of God
The growing strength of his foes
The punishment of his sins

3.question: What does Lamentations 3:40 urge the people to do?
options: Search their ways and turn again to the Lord
Immediately rebuild the destroyed walls of the city
Make a new political alliance with the Babylonians
Flee to the distant mountains of the north

3.question: In Lamentations 3:48-49, what does the speaker say of his weeping eye?
options: It is now dry from much weeping
It runs down without ceasing
It now rejoices with great joy
It sleeps calmly in peace

3.question: From where did the speaker call upon the Lord's name in Lamentations 3:55?
options: From atop the sacred mountain
From the inner court of the temple
Out of the low dungeon
From the royal hall of the palace

3.question: In Lamentations 3:57, what did the Lord say when the speaker called?
options: Be still
Go in peace
Wait yet
Fear not

3.question: How does the speaker close his plea about his enemies in Lamentations 3:64?
options: Asking the Lord to repay them according to their deeds
Pleading with the Lord to forgive them completely for their wickedness
Asking the Lord to forget them forever from his memory
Blessing them with lasting peace and great prosperity

4.title: Purer than snow
4.text: Verse 7 recalls that Zion's princes (Nazarites) were once 'purer than snow, whiter than milk' — making the next verse's picture of them blackened by famine all the more shocking.

4.question: Lamentations 4:6 says the punishment of the people is greater than the sin of which city?
options: Sodom
Nineveh
Babylon
Egypt

4.question: According to Lamentations 4:11, what did the Lord kindle in Zion?
options: A dark cloud that covered the whole city
A fire that devoured its foundations
A strong wind that scattered all his people
A plague that destroyed the crops

4.question: Lamentations 4:13 blames the city's fall on the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of whom?
options: Her kings
Her merchants
Her priests
Her soldiers

4.question: In Lamentations 4:21, to whom is it said the cup of judgment shall also pass?
options: The daughter of Egypt
The daughter of Babylon
The daughter of Moab
The daughter of Edom

5.question: How does Lamentations 5:3 describe the people?
options: Orphans and fatherless
Lords of the land and people
Valiant and honored warriors
Priests of the temple

5.question: In Lamentations 5:6, to which two nations did they give the hand for bread?
options: Babylon and Persia
Egypt and Assyria
Moab and Edom
Tyre and Sidon

5.question: How does Lamentations 5:19 describe the Lord, in contrast to the ruined nation?
options: He changed his purpose; his throne was destroyed for ever
He turned away from us for ever; his throne became empty and forgotten
He remains for ever; his throne from generation to generation
He grew weary of his people and abandoned his throne

5.title: An ending read twice
5.text: Because the book ends on a somber note, Jewish tradition repeats the hopeful plea 'Turn thou us unto thee, O Lord... renew our days as of old' — so the public reading ends on hope.
